title: CRLA/44/2012 of AMARJEET SINGH Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 44 of 2012
Amarjeet Singh. ÖÖ.Appellant.
Versus
State of Uttarakhand. Ö......Ö. Respondent.
Present:
Mr. Bhaskar Chandra Joshi, Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. Vipul Painuly, AGA with Mr. Prabhakar Joshi and Mr. K.S. Rangarh, Brief Holder for the State.
With
Criminal Appeal No. 59 of 2012
Om Prakash. ÖÖ.Appellant.
Versus
State of Uttarakhand. Ö......Ö. Respondent.
Present:
Mr. D.C.S. Rawat, Advocate holding brief of Mr. T.K. Nailwal, Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. Vipul Painuly, AGA with Mr. Prabhakar Joshi and Mr. K.S. Rangarh, Brief Holder for the State.
Honíble Alok Singh, J (Oral).
1. At the outset, it is pertinent to mention here that
in compliance of Courtís order dated 12.04.2013 Sub Inspector
Bhupal Singh, police station Banbasa, District Champawat has
produced two sealed packets for perusal of this Court. Both
packets were opened in the Court. After examination, currency
notes were again kept in sealed covers and handed over to Mr.
Prabhakar Joshi, Brief Holder for the State, who handed over
the same to Sub Inspector Bhupal Singh, in the presence of this
Court.
2. Appellants have preferred this appeal against the
judgment and order dated 08.02.2012 passed by Sessions Judge,
Champawat in Sessions Trial No. 2 of 2007 whereby both the
appellants were convicted under Section 489-C IPC and

2
sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for the period of
three years each and to pay fine of Rs. 10,000/- each, and in
default of making payment of fine, to undergo additional
imprisonment of six months under Section 489-C IPC.
3. Brief facts of the present case, inter alia, are that
PW 1 Sub Inspector Neeraj Kumar along with Constable
Mubarak Hasan, Constable Ganesh Singh, Constable Arvind
Kumar left the police station Banbasa, District Champawat on
17.01.2006 at about 02.40 p.m. vide report no. 21 for patrolling
duty; when police party reached near Patni Trijunction
(TIRAHA), police informer passed on secret information to the
effect that two persons were standing near Meena Bazar,
having counterfeit and fictitious Indian currency notes; both of
them were intending to use them in the market and also
intending to exchange the same with some Nepali citizen,
therefore, police could arrest them; having received such secret
information, police personnel searched each other and having
satisfied that none of them was having any illegal thing
proceeded towards Meena Bazar along with police informer;
when police party reached near Forest Check Post, police
informer pointed out towards two persons standing on
unmetalled road and told the police party that those persons
were having counterfeit and fictitious currency notes; police
party proceeded towards unmetalled road, however, having
noticed the police party, both of them rushed towards the
Forest; police party asked them to stop, however, they did not
stop and started running towards the Forest; after chasing them
for almost 200 metres, both of them were apprehended and on
being asked, both of them started apologizing and told the
police party that they were carrying fictitious and counterfeit
Indian currency notes; both of them disclosed their identity to

3
the police party; search was conducted, from the pocket of
jacket wore by Om Prakash 87 counterfeit currency notes of 100
denomination were recovered while from the left pocket of
jacket wore by Amarjeet 6 counterfeit currency notes of 100
denomination were recovered.
4. Having seen the currency notes, so recovered
from both the appellants, police party came to the conclusion
that all the currency notes, recovered from the appellants, were
fictitious and counterfeit, therefore, seizure memo, containing
the details of the currency notes, was prepared on the spot;
appellants were formally arrested and their arrest memos were
also prepared on the spot; currency notes, so recovered from
the appellants, were kept in different seal covers under the
seals and signatures of Arresting Officer and sample seal was
also prepared on the spot; currency notes, so recovered, and
appellants were brought to the police station and report was
lodged with police station Banbasa, District Champwat,
thereupon, check FIR no. 1 of 2006 was got registered. Initially,
investigation was handed over to Inspector Vipin Chandra Pant
(PW4), however, later on, it was handed over to Inspector
Naresh Chandra (PW5).
5. Having investigated the matter, a charge-sheet
was submitted against the appellants for the offence punishable
under Section 489-C IPC. After committal of the trial, both the
appellants were charged for the offence punishable under
Section 489-C IPC. Both the appellants denied charge and
claimed trial.
6. It is important to mention here that meanwhile,
another charge-sheet was submitted against one Mohd. Haneef

4
from whom both the appellants allegedly received these
counterfeit currency notes, however, Mohd. Haneef died
during the pendency of trial, therefore, trial against him stood
abated.
7. In order to prove its case, from the side of
prosecution, PW1 Sub Inspector Neeraj Kumar (Arresting
Officer), PW2 Constable Arvind Kumar, PW3 Constable
Laxman Chand, PW4 Vipin Chandra Pant, PW5 Inspector
Naresh Chand and PW6 Dhirender Kumar were examined.
Statements of appellants were also recorded under Section 313
Cr.P.C.
8. Learned trial court, having perused the entire
material made available on record, vide impugned judgment
and order, convicted and sentenced the appellants, as
mentioned hereinabove.
9. I have heard Mr. D.C.S. Rawat and Mr. B.C.
Joshi, learned counsel for the appellants and Mr. Vipul Painuly,
AGA with Mr. Prabhakar Joshi and Mr. K.S. Rangarh, Brief
Holders for the State and have carefully perused the record.
10. As per the statement of Arresting Officer Sub
Inspector Neeraj Kumar (PW1), he had kept the counterfeit and
fictitious currency notes, so recovered from the appellants, in
seal covers under his seals and signatures; sample seal was also
prepared on the spot; after reaching to the police station, seal
covers, containing the counterfeit and fictitious currency notes,
so recovered from the appellants, sample seal, prepared on the
spot, seizure memo and arresting memo were handed over to
the Constable present in the police station and thereafter, check

5
FIR was lodged and materials, related to the case, were kept in
the Maalkhana of the police station.
11. PW4 Investigating Officer Inspector Vipin
Chandra Pant stated that on 07.04.2006, currency notes were
sent to Nasik Currency Press for examination under the orders
of court. However, during his cross-examination, he stated as
under:
ìApplication moved by him, for examination of
counterfeit and fictitious currency notes recovered
from the appellants, before this court is not
available on record; I had filed the charge-sheet
against the accused before I could get the report of
FSL; application and permission of the court for
examination of the currency notes recovered from
the appellants is not available on record.î
12. With the help of learned counsel for the
appellants and learned State counsel, I have carefully perused
the record. There is nothing on record on show under whose
order and authority currency notes, so recovered, from the
appellants, were sent to Nasik Currency Press for examination.
13. Even, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
State before this Court, are not able to point out the order or
authority under which counterfeit currency notes were
forwarded to the Nasik Currency Press for examination to find
out the genuineness of the currency notes, so recovered from
the appellants.
14. PW2 Constable Arvind Kumar, during his cross-examination, (at page 58 of the paper book) stated that Sub

6
Inspector Neeraj Kumar (PW1) deposited the currency notes, so
recovered from the appellants, in the police station but he does
not remember with whom he had deposited the currency notes,
so recovered from the appellants.
15. PW4 Investigating Officer, during his cross-examination, (at page no. 70 of the paper book) stated that he
never saw, the currency notes, so recovered from the appellants
and charge-sheet was submitted by him without looking into
the currency notes, so recovered from the appellants. (At page
70 of the paper book) he further stated that sample seal is not
available on record and he cannot say under whose seal and
signature currency notes were kept in the seal cover.
16. PW6 Station Officer, Dhirender Kumar, during
his cross-examination (at page no. 75 of the paper book), stated
that packet, which had been taken by him to the Nasik
Currency Press for examination, was not present in the court.
17. In the present case, entries of Maalkhana register
were also not produced to prove that at what time and on
which date, currency notes, kept in the seal covers under the
seals and signatures of PW1 and sample seal of PW1 were
deposited in the Maalkhana. In absence of entries of the
Maalkhana Register, it would be difficult to say, as to how and
when seal covers and sample seal were kept in the Maalkhana,
how and when same came out from Maalkhana and for what
purpose.
18. In the firm opinion of this Court, entries of
Maalkhana register are very important piece of link evidence.
PW3, during his cross-examination (at page no. 64 of the paper
book) stated that sample seal, prepared by PW1, was not

7
available on record. In the same fashion, PW4 Investigating
Officer, Vipin Chandra Pant (at page no. 70 of the paper book)
stated that sample seal was not available on the record and he
did not know under whose seal and signature, currency notes
were kept in the seal covers.
19. In the opinion of this Court, in the absence of
sample seal and in absence of entries of Maalkhana register,
prosecution has failed to prove that currency, so recovered
from the appellants, remained intact and in the absence of any
application and order thereon to send the counterfeit currency
notes for examination to Nasik Currency Press, it cannot be
said that currency, so recovered from the appellants, were in
fact, sent to Nasik for examination.
20. PW1 Searching and Arresting Officer, Sub
Inspector Neeraj Kumar, during his cross-examination (at page
44 of the paper book) stated that he had not arrested the
appellants while they were purchasing anything by paying
counterfeit currency notes. In the same fashion, PW4,
Investigating Officer Inspector Vipin Chandra Pant (at page 69
of the paper book) stated that he had not seen the appellants
using counterfeit currency notes, so recovered from their
possession.
21. Perusal of the statements of prosecution
witnesses suggests that appellants were not having any
knowledge that they were carrying counterfeit or fictitious
currency notes. None of them stated that they ever tried or
were intending to use fictitious or counterfeit currency notes
allegedly recovered from their possession.

8
22. In the firm opinion of this Court, floating
statements to the effect that police informer had informed the
police party that appellants were standing near Patni
Trijunction (TIRAHA) and were intending to use fictitious
currency notes is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the
appellants for the offence punishable under Section 489-C IPC.
23. Honíble Apex Court in the case of Umashakar
Vs. State of Chhattisgarh reported in AIR 2001 SC 3074 in
paragraph 8 has held as under:
ì8. A perusal of the provisions, extracted above,
shows that mens rea of offences under Section 489-
B and 489-C is, "knowing or having reason to
believe the currency-notes or bank notes are forged
or counterfeit". Without the afore-mentioned mens
rea selling, buying or receiving from another
person or otherwise trafficking in or using as
genuine forged or counterfeit currency-notes or
bank-notes, is not enough to constitute offence
under Section 489-B of I.P.C. So also possessing or
even intending to use any forged or counterfeit
currency-notes or bank-notes is not sufficient to
make out a case under Section 489-C in the
absence of the mens rea, noted above. No material
is brought on record by the prosecution to show
that the appellant had the requisite mens rea.î
24. As per the dictum of Honíble Apex Court to
make out case punishable under Section 489-B or 489-C IPC,
prosecution is duty bound to prove mens rea on the part of the
accused by saying that accused was selling, buying or receiving
the counterfeit or fictitious currency notes or even intending to

9
use the fictitious currency notes and accused was having
requisite knowledge that he was carrying fictitious or
counterfeit currency notes with intention to use them in the
market.
25. As observed herein above, prosecution has
miserably failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Consequently, appeals are allowed. Impugned judgment and
order dated 08.02.2012 passed by Sessions Judge, Champawat
in Sessions Trial No. 2 of 2007 is hereby set aside. Both the
appellants stand acquitted of the charges levelled against them.
Appellant Amarjeet is on bail. He need not to surrender in
connection with present case. His personal bonds and sureties
are discharged. Appellant Om Prakash is in jail. Let he be
released forthwith, if not wanted in any other case.
26. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the court
below for compliance along with lower court record.
 (Alok Singh, J.)
 16.04.2013
SKS
